newsitem.title: FRANCE: French teachers strike in protest at job cuts.
newsitem.headline: French teachers strike in protest at job cuts.

text.p: French teachers began a one-day strike on Monday, disrupting many schools and forcing several to close in a protest over plans to shed some 2,300 education jobs.
Unions plan demonstrations in some 60 cities and towns, with the biggest march due in Paris through the students' Latin Quarter to the Education Ministry.
The action was the first called jointly by the country's five biggest teachers' unions in four years. They represent some 825,000 teachers.
"When you shed jobs, you make working conditions and young people's eduction worse," Michel Deschamps, secretary-general of the teachers' FSU union, told RTL radio.

The government has announced plans to eliminate more than 5,000 jobs in primary and secondary education in 1997 while creating 2,700 posts in higher education. That will mean, on balance, 2,300 fewer jobs.

The government, under fire for its budget and economic policies after unemployment reached a record 12.6 percent last month, will be closely watching the teachers as a measure of national dissatisfaction with the programme of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Labour leaders have been predicting significant unrest in the coming months, and a big civil service strike has been set for October 17.
Marc Blondel, leader of Force Ouvriere, one of France's three biggest unions, accused Juppe of failing to stay in touch with union federations.

"Since October of last year, Juppe's labour affairs adviser hasn't called me once. When you lead a country you have to be in touch with those who represent part of that country," Blondel told Europe-1 radio.

Opinion polls show Juppe's popularity ratings at near-record lows, and some deputies in the governing centre-right have begun openly pleading for a change in priorities well ahead of 1998 general elections.

But so far there has been little evidence of dissatisfaction of the magnitude that led to last year's crippling public-sector strikes, which virtually paralysed France for a four-week period during November and December.
In a separate protest, train drivers at state-owned SNCF went on strike on Monday in a protest at working hours in the eastern suburbs of Paris, cutting services by a third.
